newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile closes schools in Santiago smog crisis.
newsitem.headline: Chile closes schools in Santiago smog crisis.

text.p: Nearly a million Chilean children stayed at home on Monday after the government closed schools in Santiago for two days as a result of dangerously high smog levels in the city.

The authorities suspended preschool and primary school classes and cancelled physical education lessons in high schools after declaring an environmental "pre-emergency" in the capital for an unprecedented six days in a row.
The suspension of classes was expected to lead to a drop of 30 percent in road traffic, officials said. Traffic is one of the main causes of air pollution in Santiago.
Although smog levels dropped so sharply by Monday afternoon that officials announced the suspension of "pre-emergency" measures on Tuesday, schools will remain closed as a precaution.

Cancelling classes was one of the measures included in a new anti-smog plan announced by President Eduardo Frei on Friday to tackle air pollution in a city that is one of the most contaminated in the world.
The measures, which will cost $600 million to implement, include the toughening of restrictions on vehicles and factories and the paving of long stretches of dirt road on the city's outskirts.
Doctors demanded even greater restrictions on factories and the closure of at least half of the 5,300 industrial plants operating in the city.

"It is not fair that only ordinary citizens pay the price of decontaminating the city. Businessmen must also play their role in improving the quality of the air," Enrique Acorssi, president of the Medical College, said.
Hospitals in Santiago have been packed over the last week with hundreds of children and elderly people suffering from respiratory illnesses caused by the smog.
A hazy gray cloud usually blankets the city for much the Southern Hemisphere winter, but the situation has been made worse than usual this year by a lack of rain in recent weeks to clear the air.
Because Santiago lies in a valley surrounded by towering Andean peaks and coastal mountains, there is virtually no wind to sweep the pollution away.

A recent World Bank survey showed Santiago to be the world's sixth most polluted city in terms of levels of particles in the air, not as bad as Calcutta or Mexico City but worse than Brazil's industrial capital, Sao Paulo.
